name: PT Antam (Persero) Tbk

frontmatter.title: Antam: gold does the earning, nickel sets the price
frontmatter.summary: PT Aneka Tambang is Indonesia's state-controlled nickel, gold and alumina miner. Gold supplies about three-quarters of revenue and the group sits on net cash, yet the shares trade at a mid-single-digit multiple of our forward earnings because the market is capitalising a nickel price far below any published forecast. The nickel profile is bounded by a ten-year reserve life; the gold block carries the earnings. Our target assumes the quota discipline the government has signalled.
thesis: Nine-month EBITDA of IDR13,480.0bn and parent profit of IDR8,830.0bn are already at the level we forecast for the full year, so the rating does not depend on a recovery in volumes or prices beyond the deck [S9, S10].

At Rp2,760 the shares are a mid-single-digit multiple of our FY2026E EPS of Rp488 and trade at 1.6x the Rp1,747 of book value we forecast per share at the year end, against a life-of-asset DCF of Rp4,427 per share [S0, S9].

The government is preparing a 2027 RKAB quota cut to drain an oversupply of 800 kt against world demand of 3,500 kt, and nickel has already rallied to US$16,375/t on enforcement of ore-trading rules [S14, S15].

Gold, not nickel, is the earnings engine at about three-quarters of sales, and our model carries that block on a revenue path bound to the house gold deck and the rupiah path year by year, with the gold leg weighted at the ninety-five per cent of the block the segments actually disclose and the bear and bull cases moving it a fifth each way; the nickel line is the option we are being paid to own, not the reason the company earns money [S9, S11].

The nickel ore is not a twenty-year annuity: the profile starts at the 16,200kt nine-month production run-rate, declines at eight per cent a year and stops in 7,649kt, ten years of production inside the regulator's sub-ten-year statement on national saprolite reserves, with the shorter life run as the bear case [S17].
Base case Rp4,758 and bear case Rp3,355 both sit above today's price; the distribution is wide because the quota decision is binary, not because the base case needs a bull price [S15].

blocks.text: **BUY; twelve-month target Rp4,894, a total return of 89.7% from Rp2,760.** The target is the engine's own arithmetic, not a multiple we chose: the life-of-asset DCF value today is Rp4,427, rolling that forward at the cost of equity and deducting the next twelve months' dividend of Rp342 gives the base case of Rp4,758, and probability-weighting the business scenarios gives Rp4,894. The gap to the price is large because the market is applying a trough multiple to a company whose earnings have already stepped up, and because the whole value sits in a life-of-asset DCF that a single-year multiple cannot see.

What Antam owns is a diversified Indonesian mining and metals platform under state control. In the nine months to September 2026 the group sold IDR88,480.0bn of goods, of which gold was IDR68,410.0bn and the nickel segment IDR16,980.0bn, with bauxite and alumina contributing IDR2,640.0bn [S9]. That mix is the first thing a nickel-focused reader gets wrong: the company is classified as a nickel name because nickel ore and ferronickel drive its incremental margin, but roughly three-quarters of its revenue is gold, sold both from its own mine and through its refinery and retail bullion franchise [S9, S11]. The nickel business is the swing factor in the valuation; it is not the whole business.

The earnings step-up is recent, sourced and large. Nine-month EBITDA reached IDR13,480.0bn, up almost half on the prior year on revenue of IDR88,480.0bn, with operating profit of IDR12,050.0bn and gross profit of IDR15,560.0bn [S9]. Group net profit was IDR9,660.0bn and parent profit IDR8,830.0bn, the latter up almost half year on year [S9, S10, S11]. Our FY2026E EBITDA of IDR17,406.5bn is therefore not a forecast leap: it is within a few per cent of the nine-month run-rate with an ordinary fourth quarter on top, and it leaves an EBITDA margin of 15.3% on the 17.6% gross margin and 4.0% SG&A the nine-month release reports [S9]. We do not compare it with the data pack's FY2025 figure of IDR7,143.2bn: that line carries a D&A charge of IDR168.1bn that is roughly one-eleventh of the LK-implied annual charge, so the audited-year comparison would be a comparison with a wrong number [S0, S9].

What the market appears to price is a nickel price that does not exist in any published forecast. The engine's reverse DCF, which solves for the flat nickel price that justifies today's share price while holding everything else at our base case, returns US$7,789 a tonne [S0]. That is a little over two-fifths of the FY2027E deck of US$17,500, below the US$15,400/t print of early November and far below where the tape has been trading since the ore-trading crackdown began [S14, S15]. The market is free to take that view, but it is a view about Indonesian supply policy, not about the earnings the company has already reported.

The policy direction is the reason we do not adopt it. The government has said it will cut the 2027 nickel ore quota, modelled on the coal quota discipline that lifted coal prices, and it frames the problem explicitly: an oversupply of 800 kt against world demand of 3,500 kt [S15]. The 2026 record shows the ministry moving both ways: the quota was first set at 250,000-260,000kt and then revised UP to 290,000-300,000kt, still below the 379,000kt actually produced in 2025 [S11, S16]. Antam kept its own ore production guidance at 18,000kt but produced 12,160kt in the nine months, so the guidance is above the realised run-rate [S9, S11]. A quota that binds is a supply cut with a government's signature on it, and that is a different object from a price forecast.

The construction is deliberately blunt about what the base case does not assume. Volume is 14,300kt of ore sold in FY2026E, then steps to the 16,200kt nine-month production run-rate as the stock built in 2026 clears, and from there the profile declines at eight per cent a year to 7,649kt and stops — ten years of production, inside the regulator's statement that national saprolite reserves support less than ten years of output and with no company mine plan in the archived record to justify anything longer [S17]. The nickel price follows the house deck from US$17,089 in FY2026E to US$17,500 in FY2027E and US$17,500 in the long run. The gold and bauxite block, four fifths of FY2026E revenue, is bound to the house gold deck — US$4,494 in FY2026E falling to US$4,300 — and the rupiah path, with the gold leg at the ninety-five per cent of block revenue the segments disclose, so the rupiah's depreciation is largely offset by the deck's gold correction rather than compounding it; the year-by-year arithmetic is in the valuation section's reconciliation table, not in a footnote. Operating working capital is held at the FY2025 ratio of 10.0% of revenue, and the DCF carries no terminal value. The result is a value that rises with the deck and falls with the rupiah, and a bear case at Rp3,355 that cuts the nickel price by a fifth, runs a shorter reserve life (volume at three quarters, about seven and a half years), cuts the gold and bauxite block's revenue by a fifth and lifts the working-capital intensity — still above today's price, which is the honest measure of how much of the target is cyclical hope.

The two cross-checks are shown, and they no longer set the target. EV/EBITDA and P/BV are struck on last-twelve-month accounting that pre-dates the 2026 earnings step-up, and both apply peer multiples earned on other companies' trough earnings. That is the classic failure mode for a cyclical, which is why the method weights give the life DCF the whole value and the multiples are a diagnostic rather than a valuation. A reader who insists on the trough-multiple view should own the stock only near the bear case value, and that is the risk the target carries.

PT Aneka Tambang Tbk, known as Antam, is an Indonesian state-controlled mining and metals company listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange and held through the state mining holding company MIND ID [S12]. The pack records insiders at 66.4% of the shares and a free float of 34.8% [S0], with a market capitalisation of IDR66,324.9bn at the last close of Rp2,760 [S0]. It employs 3,828 people and trades IDR306.3bn a day, so the register is liquid enough for institutional positions despite the state block [S0]. The company reports in rupiah and its shares are priced in rupiah, which matters because its revenue is effectively dollar-linked.

The business runs in four lanes. Nickel is ore plus ferronickel from the Kolaka and Pomalaa smelting operations in Sulawesi, fed by the company's own laterite mines [S9, S11]. Gold runs from the Pongkor underground mine through a refinery and into its retail bullion business, which is why gold revenue of IDR68,410.0bn in nine months dwarfs what a single mine could produce: a large part of it is metal bought, refined and resold [S9, S12]. Bauxite and alumina run from the Kijang mine into chemical-grade alumina and, through the Mempawah smelter-grade alumina refinery built with Inalum, into the aluminium chain [S12]. A small fourth lane covers other minerals and services [S9]. The revenue mix in the nine months to September was gold at IDR68,410.0bn, nickel at IDR16,980.0bn and bauxite and alumina at IDR2,640.0bn [S9].

The operating data show how differently the two big lanes behaved this year. Nickel ore production was 12,160 kt wmt against sales of 10,730 kt wmt, so the company mined more than it shipped and built stock [S9]. Ferronickel production was 11.64kt of contained nickel against sales of 13.97kt, so sales ran ahead of output and the company drew down inventory — and sales were up sharply on the 8.18kt sold in the same period of 2025 [S9]. In the first half the pattern was the same in miniature: ore production well above ore sales, with ferronickel sales of a similar order and a gold volume that reflects the retail franchise [S2]. The reconciliation matters for the forecast: ferronickel revenue growth is partly an inventory release rather than a production success, and ore sales sit below production. Our model folds ferronickel into the nickel revenue capture rather than carrying a separate ferronickel volume line, so the release is inside the FY2026E calibration and does not repeat because the capture is held flat thereafter; the cost of that simplification is that the nickel sensitivity applies to the blended ore-plus-ferronickel line rather than to the two products separately, which we disclose rather than hide.

Guidance and quotas frame the volume line. Antam has kept its nickel ore production guidance at 18,000kt for the year, but produced 12,160kt in the nine months, a run-rate below the guidance [S9, S11]. The national quota history is a record of loosening inside 2026, not only of cuts: the initial 2026 quota was 250,000-260,000kt, the revised quota 290,000-300,000kt, and 2025 actual output 379,000kt [S11, S16]. The ministry says it is evaluating a further cut for 2027, but no 2027 quota has been issued [S16]. Antam's own share of national output is therefore in the low single digits by volume, which cuts both ways: the company is too small to set the price, but it is also a priority holder of a state allocation in a regime where the allocation is the scarce asset.

The strategy is downstream integration rather than volume growth. The Gresik precious-metals plant is designed for up to five million gold bars a year and roughly thirty tonnes of fine-gold processing capacity, which moves the gold business further into refining and branded product [S12]. On nickel, the company is developing an electric-vehicle battery chain from mining through processing to battery materials, and on bauxite the Mempawah smelter-grade alumina refinery is being built with Inalum as part of the national aluminium integration [S12]. None of these projects is separately valued in our model because no archived source gives a project value or a completion date, and we will not invent one; they are treated as inside the capex intensity and as upside optionality. The non-operating investment balance in the June balance sheet is a different set of assets — the group's associates and other holdings carried at reported value — and it enters the equity bridge separately; it is not the Gresik or Mempawah spend, which sits in fixed assets and inside the capex line [S0, S9, S12]. The archived record does not itemise that portfolio, so we carry the reported balance and disclose the opacity rather than zero it.

Market position is best described as a national champion with a commodity cost position. Antam is the listed vehicle through which the state holds its nickel, gold and bauxite interests, and it sells most of its output domestically — 95.0% of nine-month sales were domestic, which is unusual for an Indonesian miner and reflects the gold retail franchise and domestic smelter demand [S11]. It is a price-taker on nickel, where the government sets a monthly ore reference price and the LME sets the metal benchmark, and a price-taker on gold, where the London fix does the work [S14]. What it controls is cost, allocation and the retail franchise, not price.

Nickel ore comes in two geological flavours. Saprolite is higher grade and is smelted into ferronickel or nickel pig iron for stainless steel; limonite is lower grade and is leached into mixed hydroxide precipitate for batteries. Indonesia banned raw ore exports and required domestic processing, which is why the country now dominates global supply and why its quota policy moves the world price. Ferronickel is sold on contained nickel, so a smelter's revenue depends on both the ore grade and the metal price, while its cost is dominated by ore, energy and reductant. The government publishes a monthly ore reference price, the HPM, which is derived from the LME and the ore's grade and moisture, so ore revenue tracks the metal price with a grade-driven wedge. Gold is simpler: mine output is refined to bars and sold at the international price, and a retail franchise adds a fabrication and brand margin on top.

Indonesia is the swing supplier of nickel and it has decided to act like one. The 2026 national ore quota was first set at 250,000-260,000kt, revised UP to 290,000-300,000kt, and still sits below 379,000kt of actual 2025 output [S11, S16]. The energy ministry is evaluating a further cut for 2027 and explicitly borrowing the playbook it used on coal, but no 2027 quota has been issued [S16]. The rationale is stated in plain language by the minister: world demand is about 3,500 kt a year and supply exceeds it by roughly 800 kt, which is why the price fell below the sixteen-thousand-dollar line [S15]. The enforcement arm has moved too: a forest-area task force is taking action against companies affiliated with a major ore trader, on suspicion of illegal activity in forest areas, which is the proximate cause of the November price spike [S14].

The price path in the record is a policy series, not a demand series. Nickel traded at US$15,400/t on 2 November, then jumped to US$16,375/t on 5 November, a five-week high, on the enforcement news [S14, S15]. The house metals deck is above both: US$15,162 for FY2025A, US$17,089 for FY2026E, US$17,500 for FY2027E and beyond, against a spot of US$16,324 [S0]. Two disclosures on that marker: the FY2027E figure is the reviewed house metals-deck marker that the engine reads, not a spot print, which is why it sits above a spot market in surplus [S0]; and the deck's long-run marker is NOMINAL and escalates with its US inflation assumption after FY2029, so the DCF does not hold a flat real price for twenty years — the sensitivity table prices the cost of the premium to spot, and the risk section carries the surplus in the bear case. The firm's macro desk tilts FAVOR to nickel and Indonesian supply-discipline names for exactly this reason, as set out in the firm's brief for this ticker. Our forecasts use the deck rather than spot.

Demand is the part the bulls overstate and the bears understate. Nickel goes into stainless steel first and batteries second, and the battery story has been the source of most of the forecast error of the last cycle [S14]. The marginal supply is Indonesian, much of it funded and operated by Chinese groups, and those producers are now discussing output cuts of their own as prices and costs squeeze them — Tsingshan, GEM, Lygend and Huayou are named in the record [S11]. A market where both the host government and the dominant producers want less volume is a market with a supply floor under it, which is the asymmetry this initiation is trying to capture.

The regulatory stack is layered and each layer can move the price. The RKAB is the annual work plan and budget that sets how much ore a company may mine, so a quota cut is a direct volume instruction rather than an incentive [S15]. On top of that sit the ore-trading rules whose enforcement triggered the November rally, royalty obligations, and the forest-area rules that the task force is now policing [S14]. For Antam the stack cuts both ways: its own volumes depend on the RKAB it receives, its realised ore price is set by the monthly HPM reference derived from the LME, and its gold business sits outside the nickel regime altogether [S9, S11]. That diversification is a genuine portfolio benefit in a policy-driven commodity.

The competitive landscape has two tiers. The first is the large Indonesian nickel complexes, mostly Chinese-funded and integrated into stainless or battery chains, which set the marginal cost and the export flow [S11]. The second is the state-linked miners such as Antam and its peers, which hold long-dated allocations and sell into domestic smelters and the domestic gold market [S9, S11]. Antam's ore output of roughly 18,000kt against national output of 379,000kt makes it a small-volume, high-visibility participant: it cannot move the national quota, but it is a reliable allocation holder with a smelter and a refinery attached. Among listed peers the model's comparison set includes the nickel producers and the diversified miners whose multiples we show in the valuation section [S0].

The moat is allocation plus integration, and it is narrower than it looks. Antam's advantages are a state mandate, an ore body administered under a national quota that its controlling shareholder sets, three ferronickel plants with contracted power from PLN, and a gold refinery and retail brand that no other Indonesian miner matches [S11, S12]. Its disadvantages are scale in nickel ore, a cost position that depends on strip ratios we cannot observe, and the governance that comes with state ownership. The five forces are unfavourable on the nickel side: buyers are few and price is benchmarked, suppliers of ore are the company itself plus a contested artisanal market, substitution between nickel pig iron and ferronickel is real, and rivalry is intense among quota holders [S15]. On the gold side the forces are better because the retail franchise carries a brand, but the metal is still a commodity.

Two external variables sit on top of the commodity. The first is the rupiah: the deck runs the dollar from 17,570 in FY2026E to 18,350 in FY2027E and 19,000 in the long run against a spot of 18,103 [S0]. Because revenue is dollar-linked and much of the cost base is rupiah, a weaker rupiah flatters the margin, and the deck already assumes depreciation. The second is energy: the ferronickel smelters buy power from PLN under a long-term agreement signed for the Kolaka plant, so coal prices pass through with a lag rather than directly, which is why we set the fuel share of the mining cost at 15% rather than the template default [S11].

The five-year record is a commodity cycle with a currency overlay. Revenue fell from IDR45,930.4bn in FY2022 to IDR41,047.7bn in FY2023, recovered to IDR69,192.4bn and reached IDR84,642.4bn in FY2025, a gain of 22.3% [S0]. EBITDA followed the same shape at a lower level — IDR2,826.3bn in the trough, IDR3,656.2bn and IDR7,143.2bn — and parent profit went from IDR3,821.0bn to IDR7,208.8bn with EPS of Rp300 [S0]. Book equity grew every year and net debt was negative throughout: the company has been in a net cash position for the whole record, which is unusual for a capital-intensive miner and is the single most important fact about its balance sheet [S0]. One line in that history is wrong and we say so: the pack's FY2025A EBITDA of IDR7,143.2bn sits below the IDR9,330.0bn the company itself reported for the first nine months of 2025 [S9], which is impossible for a full year of the same scope. The cause is the pack's D&A line, and until the FY2025 LK is archived we treat the nine-month figure as the floor for the year rather than presenting the pack's number as audited history [S0, S9].

The reported D&A line in the data pack is wrong and the model corrects it in the forecast. The pack carries FY2025 D&A of IDR168.1bn for a group with three ferronickel smelters, an alumina refinery and a gold mine — an implausibly small charge for that asset base. The company's own release gives the true size without needing an estimate: the gap between nine-month EBITDA of IDR13,480.0bn and operating profit of IDR12,050.0bn is the depreciation and amortisation charged in the income statement, and annualising that charge gives IDR1,900.0bn a year [S9, F14, F15]. We apply that charge in every forecast year through the per-unit input, so forecast EBITDA and cash flow are internally consistent, but the historical EBITDA line in the table inherits the pack's understatement and should be read as a floor rather than a level [S0].

The nine-month actuals are the calibration point. Revenue of IDR88,480.0bn was up sharply on the IDR72,030.0bn of the prior year, gross profit was IDR15,560.0bn, operating profit IDR12,050.0bn and EBITDA IDR13,480.0bn [S9]. Group net profit was IDR9,660.0bn and the parent share IDR8,830.0bn, with the gap explained by the minority interests in the operating subsidiaries, which our model charges at 8.6% of net profit [S9, S10]. Operating cash flow was IDR5,060.0bn, cash rose to IDR10,540.0bn and equity to IDR41,220.0bn, while gross debt stayed around IDR5,740.0bn at the half year [S9, S2].

The trend inside the nine months is less flattering than the headline and the forecast respects it. First-half revenue was IDR62,710.0bn and group net profit IDR6,910.0bn [S2]; subtracting those from the nine-month figures leaves a third quarter that contributed materially less than the first half's quarterly run-rate [S9, S11]. Two things explain it: nickel prices were weaker into the quarter, and the ferronickel inventory release that flattered the first half could not repeat [S9, S15]. Our FY2026E numbers assume a fourth quarter at roughly the third quarter's level, not a return to the first half's, which is why FY2026E parent profit of IDR11,732.0bn sits only modestly above the nine-month actual [S0].

The forecast is a five-line build. Volume is 14,300kt of ore sold in FY2026E, the nine-month sales annualised with an ordinary fourth quarter; from FY2027E sales rise to 16,200kt, the nine-month production run-rate, because the company produced more ore than it sold in 2026 and the stock must clear [S9, F1, F2], and then decline at eight per cent a year to 7,649kt as the reserve life runs out [S17]. The realisation is 0.43% of the LME price per tonne of ore sold, a grade and payability ratio rather than a discount: ore is priced on contained metal at the government's HPM reference, and a tonne of ore carries a fraction of a tonne of nickel [S9]. Unit cash cost is US$37.1 a tonne, of which mining is 27 dollars and the haul, port and processing residual 8 dollars, with a fuel share of 15% [S9, S11]. The non-nickel businesses — gold, bauxite and alumina — start at IDR95,330.0bn of revenue and a 16.1% gross margin, and that block then follows the house gold deck and the rupiah path year by year rather than being frozen — the template reads one price driver, so the deck path is bound into the revenue values with the arithmetic shown in the valuation section and flexed in the scenarios rather than read live by the engine [S9, S0]. Operating working capital is held at 10.0% of revenue, the FY2025 gross ratio, so the cash flow carries the working-capital absorption the nine-month accounts actually show [S0, S9].

That build produces revenue of IDR113,792.9bn in FY2026E, an increase of 34.4%, and EBITDA of IDR17,406.5bn at a margin of 15.3% [S0]. The margin is above the nine-month 2025 run-rate because the gold block earns a better spread at current prices, the nickel price is above the depressed FY2025 average of US$15,162, and the fixed cost base is spread over more revenue [S0, S9]. The cost lines are the ones the LK shows: a 17.6% gross margin and SG&A at 4.0% of sales, so EBITDA is the residual of sourced lines rather than of a plug [S9]. Revenue in FY2027E of IDR117,854.6bn grows 3.6% as ore sales reach the production run-rate and the gold block follows the deck and the rupiah; after that the declining ore profile broadly offsets the block's rupiah conversion and inflation escalation, so revenue is flat rather than compounding — which is what a ten-year reserve life and a flat production plan imply, not a forecast of absent demand [S0, S17].

Cost behaviour is the part we are least able to observe and have handled with the simplest defensible rule. The template prices mining cost as a strip ratio times a cost per cubic metre, and we use the strip-ratio input as a cost-intensity factor of 1.0 rather than as a physical ratio, because no archived source discloses Antam's actual strip [S9]. The consequence is that a higher strip ratio in reality would raise cost and lower value, and the sensitivity table prices a fifteen per cent swing in that intensity. Fuel is only 15% of mining cost because the energy-intensive step is smelting, which buys power from PLN under contract rather than burning diesel at the mine [S11]. Royalty is the template constant because no archived source states the effective rate, and we flag that rather than pretending to a statutory number [S0].

Cash conversion is the weakest line in the accounts and the model now carries it. Nine-month operating cash flow of IDR5,060.0bn against EBITDA of IDR13,480.0bn is a conversion rate well below one, and the bridge is explicit: operating cash flow is EBITDA less cash tax, less the working-capital build, plus net interest [S9, F14, F20]. The build is the dominant term: inventory and receivables rise with the gold trading business, and the company has been stockpiling ore while selling ferronickel out of inventory [S9]. Our model holds operating working capital at 10.0% of revenue — the FY2025 gross ratio of inventory plus receivables less payables — which implies a build of IDR7,169.6bn in FY2026E and free cash flow of IDR5,790.7bn against EBITDA of IDR17,406.5bn [S0]. That is the same order of conversion the nine-month accounts show; the residual difference is the tax and interest timing inside operating cash flow and the fourth-quarter collection season, for which no archived source supports a release. The gap is the price of growth in a trading-heavy revenue mix, and it is why the DCF value is below what an EBITDA multiple would suggest if working capital were ignored.

Capex and capital allocation are conservative relative to the cash generated. FY2025 capex of IDR699.4bn was low even for a sustaining year, and we forecast IDR1,500.0bn a year, which is a little over 1.3% of revenue and well under half of EBITDA [S0]. That covers sustaining spend at the mine, the smelters and the refinery but not a separately valued expansion; the Gresik and Mempawah projects are inside it and are disclosed as upside optionality rather than valued [S12]. On the distribution side the company declared IDR5,040.0bn for FY2025, a payout of 70% of earnings, and our FY2026E dividends paid of IDR5,046.2bn reconcile to that declaration because the model applies the same payout to the prior year's profit [S3, S0]. The forecast dividend per share is Rp342, a yield of roughly one eighth of today's price, and it is covered more than comfortably by free cash flow [S0].

The balance sheet has no leverage problem. Net debt was IDR-6,155.0bn at the FY2025 year end and the model carries net cash of IDR-6,677.1bn by the FY2026E year end as cash accumulates, with gross debt held flat at IDR4,556.9bn because no refinancing or new facility is disclosed [S0, S2]. Return on equity is 30.4% in FY2026E and stays above twenty per cent through the forecast, which for a commodity producer at deck prices is the clearest statement that the business earns its cost of capital with room to spare [S0]. The DCF is struck on the 30 September balance sheet, not the June one: the pack's latest balance sheet is dated 30 June, and the third quarter's net cash build is carried as an explicit bridge item, cash of 10,540 IDR bn against gross debt last disclosed at 5,740 IDR bn taking net cash above the pack's June figure [S0, S9, S2].

The earnings-quality flags we would put in front of a portfolio manager are these. First, sales are running ahead of production in ferronickel, so part of the revenue growth is inventory release rather than output [S9]. Second, cash conversion is below profit because of working capital, which we treat as structural to the gold trading mix [S9, S11]. Third, the group result carries a minority charge that takes roughly a tenth of net profit away from parent shareholders [S9, S10]. Fourth, the state is both controlling shareholder and policy-maker, so the dividend and the quota are set in the same building. Fifth, the historical D&A line in the data pack is understated by an order of magnitude, which distorts any historical multiple computed from it [S0]. None of these changes the base case; together they explain why we lean on cash flow and disclosed operating data rather than on reported EBITDA history.

The method set fits a commodity producer whose value is the ore it can economically extract. The primary method is a life-of-asset discounted cash flow with no terminal value: the nickel ore profile is exhausted inside the forecast, so the ore value is a finite annuity that ends, and what remains afterwards is the gold refinery and retail franchise, which earns a spread rather than a mine margin and is carried for the rest of the template horizon rather than capitalised in perpetuity [S0, S9]. That is the right anchor for a business whose earnings depend on a benchmark price, and it avoids the trap of capitalising a single year's margin. The cost of capital is built bottom-up, and the arithmetic is shown so it can be checked: a risk-free rate of 7.4% on Indonesian government debt less a default spread of 1.6% (the sovereign is not risk-free in rupiah), a mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2%, a country risk premium of 2.5%, an unlevered beta of 1.10 from the industry configuration levered to 1.18 at gearing of 0.09, and a 1.5% state-control governance premium; that gives a cost of equity of 15.2%, a cost of debt of 9.4% and a weighted average cost of capital of 14.6% at a 91.7% equity weight [S0]. The cost of debt is the industry default, well above the company's actual interest cost, so it is prudent rather than aggressive.

The DCF produces an enterprise value of IDR92,826.8bn and, after net cash rolled to 30 September, minorities and the non-operating investment balance, an equity value of Rp4,427 per share [S0, S9]. There is no terminal value at all, so the value is not a growth assumption in disguise [S0]. Three choices drive the number. The first is volume, and it is now bounded by the reserve evidence rather than held flat: ore sales step from 14,300kt in FY2026E to 16,200kt, the production run-rate, then decline at eight per cent a year to 7,649kt and stop — ten years of production, which is the only reserve life the record supports, since the regulator puts national saprolite reserves under ten years [S17] and Antam publishes no reserve statement we could archive, its site refusing automated fetches. The engine's comparison to the FY2025 actual cannot be run because the pack carries no volume series, so the profile is anchored on the 9M2026 production and sales data instead [S9]. The shorter life is the bear case (volume at three quarters, about seven and a half years) and the longer life the bull (volume at one and a quarter times, about twelve and a half years), so the reserve-life axis is tested in the distribution rather than assumed away. The second choice is the gold block, which supplies four fifths of FY2026E revenue and most of the group's gross profit, and here the template's limit has to be stated rather than glossed: the commodity template carries one price driver, so there is no live gold line in the engine. The block is instead reconstructed from the disclosed segments and carried on the house gold deck and the rupiah path year by year, and the table below is the reconciliation a reader needs to check it: block revenue is the FY2026E annualised non-nickel sales of IDR95,330.0bn, weighted ninety-five per cent to gold (the share F9 and F11 actually show) and five per cent to bauxite/alumina, multiplied by the gold deck ratio and the rupiah ratio each year.

Gold and FX from the house decks; block revenue is the FY2026E annualised non-nickel sales carried on the gold deck and the rupiah path with the gold leg at ninety-five per cent of the block; cost of sales is revenue at the block's 16.1% gross margin. Block gross profit is revenue less cost of sales.

The block's revenue path in the table above is arithmetic, not a judgement: every year is the FY2026E block times the gold share times the change in the deck and the rupiah, the gold volume behind it is held at the disclosed 25,217 kg for nine months a year, so the leg's revenue per kilogram is the deck price plus the refining and retail spread the segment actually earns, and the block's gross margin of 16.1% is the one that reconciles the group to the 17.6% gross margin the 9M2026 accounts report [S9]. The earlier version of this report weighted the gold leg at a mixed-period ratio — nine-month gold over a full-year block — which under-weighted the deck leg and overstated every forecast year by about one per cent; the share is corrected to ninety-five per cent and the path with it. What the engine can flex is the scenario shock: the bear cuts the block's revenue by a fifth and the bull lifts it by a quarter, both on the disclosed volume, so the target is tested on a gold move of a fifth even though the engine does not read the gold deck. Run one driver at a time, a fifth off the gold block is worth more than a tenth of the twelve-month value and a fifth off the nickel price slightly more than that, while cutting the reserve life to three quarters of the profile is worth about a twentieth — so the valuation now rests on the gold deck before it rests on nickel, which is the right ranking for a company that earns four fifths of its revenue from gold. That proxy is honest but coarser than a live gold line would be, and it is the main simplification a reader must allow for. The third choice is the horizon: the twenty-year template life now carries the gold franchise after the ore runs out, with terminal value at 0.0% of the enterprise value, and about a sixth of that value sits in the years after the ore profile ends — the part a reader who thinks the gold trading spread will not last twenty years should strike out. A reader who strikes it still has a value above the price.

The two cross-checks are reported as a diagnostic, not as a weight. EV/EBITDA applies the peer median multiple to last-twelve-month EBITDA and P/BV applies a peer multiple to June book value; both come out far below the DCF, and both are struck on the trough year. The reason is mechanical: the LTM EBITDA in the data pack is the FY2025 figure of IDR7,143.2bn, struck at the bottom of the nickel price cycle and with the understated D&A line, while the DCF capitalises the earnings the company is delivering now [S0, S9]. The peer set reinforces it: the nickel names in the comparison trade on low multiples of their own trough earnings, and a median of that group is not a fair multiple for a company whose earnings mix is mostly gold [S0]. That is why the method weight is the life DCF alone and the multiples sit beside it in the table — they are measuring a different year, and a multiple the report itself calls unfair should not set part of the target.

The forward multiples show what the price is actually paying. On our FY2026E numbers the shares trade at a mid-single-digit multiple of earnings, at 1.6x our forecast year-end book value of Rp1,747 per share, which is struck on forecast FY2026E equity over 24,031 million shares, and at a dividend yield of roughly one eighth [S0, S9]. The ratio is not struck on the 30 September balance sheet: that equity of IDR41,220.0bn is a lower numerator because a quarter of retained profit is still to come, and a reader who prefers to mark the stock on the reported book should re-derive the multiple from it rather than mixing the two [S9, F24]. On FY2027E the earnings multiple falls further because profit grows and the share count does not [S0]. Those are not multiples that a net-cash, thirty-per-cent-return, state-backed miner usually commands, and the discount is the whole investment case: the market is not disputing the earnings, it is refusing to pay for them.

The sensitivity grid prices the two variables the engine reads. A ten per cent move in the nickel price moves the twelve-month value by about a seventh of the gap to the target, because the nickel line is a minority of revenue but the majority of the marginal margin; a ten per cent move in the dollar moves it by less, because the model converts revenue and escalates costs in the same currency [S0]. The volume and unit-cost grid is the one to watch if the 2027 quota is cut: a lower volume with a higher unit cost is the bear case, and the bear case is not catastrophic because the gold block carries the profit [S0]. The axis the grid cannot price is the gold deck, which is why the scenario table carries a fifth either way on the block: that shock, not the nickel one, is the largest single swing in the target.

What today's price implies is the cleanest way to state the variant view. The reverse DCF holds everything at our base case and solves for the nickel price: the answer is US$7,789 a tonne, a little over two-fifths of the FY2027E deck [S0]. No forecast in the archive is anywhere near that level; the lowest print in the record is US$15,400/t on 2 November, before the enforcement rally took it to US$16,375/t [S14, S15]. In other words, the market is not pricing a nickel cycle at all — it is pricing a permanent collapse in Indonesian ore economics, or it is applying a governance and liquidity discount that our DCF does not model. We think it is mostly the latter. The DCF value of Rp4,427 against a price of Rp2,760 quantifies the discount, and we carry part of it in the required return through a state-control governance premium in the cost of equity rather than assuming it vanishes. The dated checkpoints that can close it are the 2027 RKAB decision and the FY2026 audited accounts, both of which are in the catalyst list; a reader who thinks the discount is permanent should mark the stock to the bear case.

The regulatory risk is first-order and binary. The 2027 RKAB quota is set by ministerial decision, it applies to the company's own mines, and it can be cut for national supply-management reasons that have nothing to do with Antam's profitability [S15]. A quota below the 14,300kt we assume would cut revenue and raise unit costs at the same time, which is exactly the bear case. The offset is that the same policy that cuts volume is intended to lift price, and Antam's high-margin ore business would benefit from the price leg before it suffered the volume leg [S15]. We treat the policy as net positive but genuinely uncertain, which is why a meaningful share of the probability sits in the bear case.

The commodity risk is concentrated in a line the model flexes only indirectly. Nickel is the price driver in our build, but gold is the earnings driver. The gold block's revenue is bound to the house gold deck and the rupiah path year by year, with the arithmetic in the valuation table, but the industry template carries one price driver, so gold is not a separate deck-read line in the engine: its exposure is tested directly in the scenarios, where the bear cuts the block's revenue by a fifth and the bull lifts it by a quarter, both on the disclosed gold volume, which is the gold-price sensitivity the Sector Lead asked us to show [S9, S11]. If the gold price falls, or if competition in retail bullion narrows the spread, the group's profit falls by more than a nickel move of the same size would take it [S9, S11]. The honest disclosure is that this proxy is coarser than a deck-linked gold line would be, that the block's margin is held flat because no source discloses a gold unit cost or refining charge, and that is why the bear case carries the gold-block shock as well as the commodity, reserve-life and working-capital shocks.

The operational risks are inventory, grade and weather. Sales running ahead of production in ferronickel is a one-off that cannot repeat without a production recovery [S9]. Ore sales below production mean stock sitting on the ground, which is a working-capital cost and a quality risk if grade deteriorates [S9]. Wet-season disruption and barging delays are the standard Indonesian mining risks, and we carry a unit-cost shock in the bear case rather than a volume shock alone [S9]. Finally, the ore-trading enforcement campaign that has lifted prices is also a compliance risk for buyers of artisanal ore: the corruption watchdog has publicly warned the company to be careful when purchasing ore from small-scale miners [S12].

The financial risks are modest but not zero. The company is in net cash and generates free cash flow well above its dividend, so refinancing risk is negligible [S0, S2]. Currency is a two-sided risk: the deck assumes the rupiah weakens, which flatters rupiah revenue and margins, and a stronger rupiah would take value out of the DCF without any change in the commodity [S0]. The dividend policy of 70% of earnings is generous for a company with a capital programme, and a state shareholder facing fiscal pressure could ask for more, which would reduce the cash retained for growth [S3]. None of these threatens solvency; together they cap the re-rating.

The governance risk is the one that explains the discount. The state owns the majority through MIND ID, sets the quota, sets the ore reference price and takes the dividend [S12, S15]. Related-party dealings are structural rather than incidental: the alumina refinery is built with Inalum, a sister company under the same holding, and the battery chain is a national project [S12]. That does not make the accounts unreliable, but it does mean minority shareholders are price-takers on capital allocation. The free float of 34.8% is above the exchange minimum, so there is no forced sell-down catalyst, and the stock is liquid at IDR306.3bn a day [S0].

The three cases are built on the same four drivers, with mirrored shocks, so the table is a distribution rather than a set of stories. The bear case cuts the nickel price by a fifth, shortens the reserve life to about seven and a half years by scaling the whole ore profile to three quarters, cuts the gold and bauxite block's revenue by a fifth on the disclosed gold volume and raises the working-capital intensity — the cash-conversion lever the red team identified — and values the shares at Rp3,355; the base case is the deck with the ten-year ore profile and gives Rp4,758; the bull mirrors all four shocks the other way, running a twelve-and-a-half-year reserve life and a quarter more gold revenue, and gives Rp6,703 [S0]. Probability-weighted, the target is Rp4,894 [S0]. The base case carries half the weight because the policy direction is clear but the timing and depth of the quota cut are not, because the company's own reserve statement is not in the record and the ore life could be longer or shorter than the national reading, and because the gold block's revenue path is bound to the deck by assumption rather than read live by the engine.

The signposts that would change our view are specific. A 2027 RKAB that comes in below the 2026 national quota, or an enforcement action that removes a large ore trader, would push us toward the bull case [S14, S15]. A quota that is raised, or a Chinese producer restart that floods the market, would move us toward the bear [S11, S15]. On the company itself, a ferronickel production recovery back toward the prior year's level would confirm that the sales growth is real rather than an inventory release, and a gold margin disclosure that shows the retail spread compressing would force us to cut the block's margin [S9, S12]. Any of those would be worth an update long before the next set of full-year accounts.

Ownership is concentrated in the state and the board answers to it. MIND ID is the holding company through which the government holds its mining interests, and Antam is one of its listed operating companies [S12]. The pack records insider holdings of 66.4%, a free float of 34.8% and institutional ownership of 15.5% [S0]. The company is not on the exchange's high-concentration list in the engine's registry and the konglo overlay does not apply, so the governance analysis here is about state control rather than about a private controlling family. That distinction matters for how the discount should be read: a state block does not create a forced-seller overhang, but it does mean the dividend and the investment programme are set with national objectives in mind.

The dividend record is the clearest evidence of how the controlling shareholder behaves. For FY2025 the company declared IDR5,040.0bn, a payout of 70% of earnings, and the model's own dividend line for the following year reconciles to the same policy [S3, S0]. The payout has been high through the cycle, which is shareholder-friendly, but it also means the company runs a thinner cash buffer than a miner with a large project pipeline might choose; in this case the net cash position absorbs that [S0]. We have no archived source for the auditor's opinion or the composition of the board, and we say so rather than asserting comfort we have not verified.

Related-party arrangements are structural. The Mempawah smelter-grade alumina refinery is developed with Inalum as part of the national aluminium integration, and both companies sit under MIND ID [S12]. The electric-vehicle battery chain is described as a national project rather than a purely commercial one [S12]. These are not hidden transactions, but they are the kind of arrangement where minority shareholders depend on the controlling shareholder to price inputs and outputs fairly. The one governance red flag in the record is the anti-corruption agency's public warning that the company should be careful when buying ore from small-scale miners, which speaks to procurement controls in the ore supply chain rather than to the accounts [S12].

The environmental and social exposure is typical of Indonesian laterite mining and above average for gold. Nickel ore mining in Sulawesi has been the subject of forest-area enforcement, and the task force action that moved the nickel price in November was about illegal activity in forest areas by affiliated companies in the ore trade [S14]. Antam's own operations are long-established and permitted, but the sector's licence to operate is being contested in public, and a stricter enforcement regime is both a price support and a compliance cost. On gold, the Pongkor underground mine and the refinery carry tailings and refining obligations, and the retail franchise puts the company's brand in front of consumers, which raises the cost of any environmental incident [S12]. On the positive side, the downstream strategy — refining gold domestically, building alumina and battery materials at home — is aligned with the government's industrial policy and reduces the export of raw ore [S12].

Capital allocation has been disciplined by the standards of the sector. The company funded its dividend and its projects from operating cash flow and still ended the September period with IDR10,540.0bn of cash against gross debt of IDR5,740.0bn, the latest debt figure disclosed (30 June) [S9, S2]. There is no record of a rights issue, a buyback or a large acquisition in the archived period, and the share count of 24,031 million has been stable [S0]. The absence of dilution is worth stating explicitly because it is unusual among Indonesian commodity names of this size, and it is one of the reasons the per-share value is not leaking away.

The 2027 quota decision is the dominant catalyst and it lands before the year turns. The energy ministry has said it will cut the nickel RKAB for 2027, modelling the policy on coal, and the market has already begun to price enforcement risk after the forest-area action [S14, S15]. A cut at or below the 2026 national level would validate the supply-discipline thesis; a quota set above it would remove the main support under the price and push the shares toward our bear case [S15]. We will update on the announcement rather than wait for the quarterly results.

The results calendar gives two more checkpoints. The FY2026 audited accounts and annual report are due in the first quarter, following the FY2025 disclosure in early March 2026, and they will show whether the fourth quarter held the third quarter's run-rate and whether the D&A charge is disclosed at the level we have inferred [S12, S9]. The annual general meeting, expected in June on the pattern of the 2026 meeting, will set the FY2026 dividend and confirm the payout policy [S3]. Between those dates the monthly HPM ore reference price and the LME settlement are the high-frequency monitors, and the model's nickel sensitivity tells us what each move is worth [S14].

The operating monitors are more informative than the price for this name. Ferronickel production against sales will show whether the inventory release has run its course; ore production against the 18,000kt guidance will show whether the quota is binding; and the gold volume and block margin will show whether the deck-linked block is holding its spread [S9, S11]. Progress at the Gresik precious-metals plant and the Mempawah refinery is a medium-term catalyst that the model does not value, so any credible capital cost or commissioning date would be incremental to our target [S12]. On the negative side, any enforcement action against an Antam-affiliated supplier, or a procurement finding from the anti-corruption agency, would be a governance event rather than an earnings event and we would treat it as a discount-widening risk [S12].

bear.narrative: The RKAB cut arrives and is deeper than signalled while demand disappoints: nickel holds 20% below the deck through the forecast, the ore reserve life runs seven and a half years instead of ten (volume x0.75, cumulative ~86m t — the quota cut and a shorter reserve statement in one lever), the gold and bauxite block's revenue falls 20% — the gold deck rolling over to a trough bullion price on the disclosed volume, which is the gold-price sensitivity the Sector Lead asked to see — and working capital absorbs 20% more of revenue as inventory and receivables build, the cash-conversion risk the red team flagged. Mirrored with the bull on exactly the same four drivers.

bull.narrative: Indonesia enforces the 2027 RKAB cut and the ore-trading crackdown removes marginal supply, so nickel runs 20% above the deck; the company states reserves that support a twelve-and-a-half-year life and ore volumes run 25% above the profile as its RKAB is renewed at a higher level, the gold and bauxite block's revenue rises 25% as bullion runs to a new high on central-bank demand, and working capital absorbs 20% less of revenue as collections improve. Mirrored with the bear on the same four drivers.
